common_name: Dwarf Red Tiger Flower (Mexican Orthantha Tigridia)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed; in zones colder than 8, lift and store dry over winter like the closely related Tigridia pavonia.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this dwarf Mexican mountain species is a smaller, more compact relative of the common tiger flower, with narrow, semi-tubular, brick-red to orange blooms that stay half-cupped rather than opening flat like Tigridia pavonia. Each flower lasts only a day, but an established clump produces a long, staggered succession of blooms through summer atop wiry, pleated foliage. Give it sharp drainage and avoid summer waterlogging, since it comes from rocky highland slopes where excess moisture around the bulb causes rot; group several bulbs together for a fuller display in a rock garden or bulb frame.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift corms before fall frost. Requires dry summer dormancy.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in mild-winter zones; this taller Cape species bears larger, wide-open, star-shaped flowers than the more commonly grown Sparaxis tricolor, typically in shades of deep purple-brown, cream, or maroon with a contrasting yellow throat ringed in dark markings. It grows through the cool, wet winter months on a fan of sword-shaped leaves and goes fully dormant once the flowers fade and the soil dries out in early summer. In zones 8-10 corms can stay in the ground year-round undisturbed; elsewhere dig and store them dry over the dormant season, and plant in generous drifts among other Cape winter-growing bulbs for the best effect.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in mild-winter zones; this soft-hued Cape species carries pale creamy-white to pale yellow flowers with a small dark-ringed yellow eye, a gentler counterpart to the bold red and orange tones of Sparaxis tricolor. It is unusual among harlequin flowers for producing small bulbils along the base of its wiry flowering stems, letting established clumps spread and thicken on their own over a few seasons. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom and keep the planting dry through summer dormancy; where summers are wet or winters harsher than zone 8, lift the corms and their bulbils and store them dry for replanting in fall.
